analysis.one_liner: Boosts federal Medicaid funding for home care and raises pay for home care workers.
analysis.headline: A bill to expand Medicaid home care and lift pay for the care workforce drew 100 Democratic cosponsors but died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give states new federal money to expand Medicaid home- and community-based care, so seniors and people with disabilities can get help at home instead of entering nursing homes. States taking the money would have to expand who qualifies, update provider payment rates at least every two years, and pass those rate increases on to the low-wage workers who deliver the care. It would also make two existing programs permanent: one that moves people out of institutions and back into their communities, and one that protects the spouses of home-care recipients from being impoverished by care costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and people with disabilities who need help with daily living but sit on Medicaid home-care waiting lists or can't qualify; family caregivers who would get respite and possible paid caregiving; and the direct care workforce — home health aides and personal care attendants, mostly low-paid — who would benefit from required payment-rate updates that must be passed through as wages, plus a benchmark requiring a majority of workers to earn competitive wages and benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Home-care recipients, waitlisted seniors, low-paid care workers

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $100 million in planning grants so states can map gaps in home- and community-based care — including waitlists, worker shortages, and payment rates — and build plans to close them, while giving states that take part a 10-percentage-point boost in the federal Medicaid matching rate (up to 95%) for home care.

Requires participating states to expand financial eligibility up to federal limits, cover personal care services for all eligible populations, and support family caregivers including respite care and paid family caregiving.

Requires states to update home-care payment rates at least every two years through a transparent stakeholder process and to pass rate increases through at least proportionately to direct care workers, with a benchmark that a majority of workers receive competitive wages and benefits before federal support continues past seven years.

Makes permanent the Money Follows the Person program, which helps states move people out of nursing homes and other institutions back into home and community settings, and makes permanent Medicaid protections against spousal impoverishment for people receiving home care.
Requires each state to designate an independent HCBS ombudsman office — separate from the Medicaid agency and managed care companies — to help beneficiaries and families and report systemic problems.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an open-ended 10-percentage-point increase in the federal Medicaid match for home- and community-based services (capped at 95%) that runs indefinitely rather than through an appropriated amount, plus roughly $115 million in specific planning and administrative appropriations. States that participate must maintain their existing home-care spending, eventually expand eligibility, and cover the remainder of costs under the match; states that fail the improvement benchmarks lose the extra federal money.

drawbacks.text: The core financing is an open-ended entitlement: the bill raises the federal Medicaid matching rate by 10 points for home care with no expiration or offset, so the federal cost grows with program spending and is not capped by the bill's modest appropriations.

Enforcement of the worker-pay goals is slow and soft — the requirement that a majority of direct care workers receive competitive wages only applies starting in the 29th quarter (year seven) after a state joins, and a state that misses benchmarks simply loses the extra match rather than facing penalties.

States bear real costs: they must maintain current home-care spending, expand eligibility up to federal limits, and pay the non-federal share, and states with weak budgets could decline to participate, leaving their residents without the expansion.

Nursing homes and other institutional providers lose census and revenue as the permanent Money Follows the Person program and the match incentives deliberately shift long-term care out of institutions and into homes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The help is targeted at a large, real unmet need — people who cannot get home care and the underpaid workforce that would provide it — and the bill ties the money to concrete requirements (eligibility expansion, rate pass-throughs, wage benchmarks) rather than handing states unrestricted funds. The costs are genuine: an open-ended increase in federal Medicaid spending and new obligations on states, and the wage protections arrive slowly. On balance, the design directs the money at the people and workers it names, though a stricter timeline and a defined funding source would have made the case stronger.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee two weeks after introduction and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the Better Care Better Jobs Act on January 26, 2023, joined by Reps. Pallone, Schakowsky, and Matsui as original sponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction and, on February 3, 2023, referred onward to the Subcommittee on Health.

One hundred of the 216 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained directly, but the Medicaid status quo held, which suited the committee majority that never acted and providers and state budgets that would have faced new requirements. The people who would have been served — those on home-care waiting lists and the low-paid care workforce — got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Backers of the Medicaid status quo

for.name: Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited Pallone, Schakowsky, and Matsui as original cosponsors.

for.name: 100 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, nearly half the House Democratic caucus; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

for.name: Frank Pallone
for.role: Ranking Member, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor of the bill in his committee's jurisdiction.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill, which sat in the Health Subcommittee from February 2023 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: House leadership and committee chairs, 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Brought no Republican cosponsors forward and took no action to move the bill to the floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 100 cosponsors were House Democrats — not a single Republican signed on — and the Republican-run committee never moved the bill, so support and obstruction both fell cleanly along party lines.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and direct care providers
industries.note: The 10-point federal match increase and required two-year payment-rate updates would channel substantially more money into home care, though the bill requires that rate increases be passed through to workers, trimming what agencies could keep.

Most states deliver home care through managed care contracts, and the bill routes its expanded funding through that system — requiring that rate increases be built into managed care payment rates rather than replacing it, locking in the insurers' role as the channel for publicly funded home care.

industries.industry: Direct care workforce (home health aides and personal care attendants)
industries.note: This is a low-wage workforce, disproportionately women of color; the bill mandates payment-rate updates with proportional pass-through to workers and a year-seven benchmark that a majority earn competitive wages and benefits.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and institutional long-term care
industries.note: By making Money Follows the Person permanent and tying federal money to shifting long-term-care spending toward home settings, the bill would move Medicaid residents — and revenue — out of institutional facilities.
